title: From capillary to mitochondria
goal: Explain how O₂ diffuses from capillary to mitochondria, what myoglobin and capillary transit time do, and why training raises O₂ extraction.

steps.title: The last few micrometres
steps.text:
Once a red cell is in a muscle capillary, its O₂ still has a journey: off the haemoglobin, through the red-cell membrane, plasma, capillary wall, the gap between cells, the fibre membrane and the cytoplasm, to the [mitochondria](g:mitochondria) [[c:o2-path]].

The pressure falls steeply along that short path. In trained men working one thigh at maximum, mean capillary PO₂ was about **38 mmHg**, but the PO₂ inside the fibre, measured through myoglobin, only about **3 mmHg** [[c:po2-drop]]. Most of the drop happens across the 1–5 μm from red cell to fibre membrane.

O₂ moves by [diffusion](g:diffusion), and Fick's law of diffusion says the flow is proportional to the surface area and to the PO₂ difference [[c:fick-law]]. More capillary contact, more flux.

claims.text: O₂ moving from capillary to mitochondria must unload from haemoglobin and cross the red-cell membrane, plasma, capillary wall, interstitium, sarcolemma and cytoplasm.

evidence.quote: including the dissociation of O 2 from Hb, and diffusion through the erythrocyte membrane, plasma, capillary wall, interstitial space, sarcolemma, cytoplasm (myoglobin facilitated or by diffusion) and into the mitochondria for utilization by the cytochromes

claims.text: At maximal knee-extension exercise, mean capillary PO₂ was about 38 mmHg while myoglobin-associated (intracellular) PO₂ was about 3 mmHg: a large blood-to-cell PO₂ difference across a 1–5 μm path.

evidence.quote: Assuming a myoglobin PO2 where 50% of myoglobin binding sites are bound with O2 of 3.2 mmHg, myoglobin-associated PO2 averaged 3.1 +/- .3 (N) and 2.1 +/- .2 mmHg (H).
resulted in calculated mean capillary PO2 values of 38 +/- 2 (N) and 30 +/- 2 mmHg(H)

These data are consistent with an O2 diffusion limitation across the 1-5-microns path-length from red cell to the sarcolemma that plays a role in determining maximal muscle O2 uptake in normal humans.

claims.text: By Fick's law of diffusion, O₂ flux is directly proportional to the PO₂ gradient and to the diffusional surface area, which more capillary-to-fibre contacts increase.

evidence.quote: according to the Fick law of diffusion, the diffusive flux is directly proportional to the PO 2 gradient
This increases the diffusional surface area that, according to the Fick law of diffusion, increases the diffusive flux in a directly proportional manner.

steps.title: Myoglobin: the fibre's own carrier
steps.text:
Inside oxidative fibres sits [myoglobin](g:myoglobin), a one-unit cousin of haemoglobin. It does three jobs: it stores a little O₂, it buffers the fibre's O₂ when activity jumps, and it helps O₂ diffuse through the cytoplasm by carrying it alongside the dissolved O₂ [[c:mb-roles]].

It binds O₂ far more tightly than haemoglobin: its P50 is about **3 mmHg**, against about 27 for haemoglobin. So in the capillary, haemoglobin lets go and myoglobin takes up. In exercising thigh muscle, myoglobin was already about half unloaded at 50% of maximum and stayed so up to the maximum [[c:mb-desat]]. A half-empty myoglobin means a very low PO₂ inside the fibre, which keeps the gradient from blood to fibre large.

claims.text: Myoglobin stores O₂ in muscle, is thought to buffer intracellular O₂ when activity increases, and to facilitate intracellular O₂ diffusion.

evidence.quote: Functionally, myoglobin is well accepted as an O2-storage protein in muscle, capable of releasing O2 during periods of hypoxia or anoxia.

Myoglobin is also thought to buffer intracellular O2 concentration when muscle activity increases and to facilitate intracellular O2 diffusion by providing a parallel path that augments simple diffusion of dissolved O2.

claims.text: Myoglobin (P50 about 3.2 mmHg) was partly desaturated within 20 s even at 50% of maximum and stayed about 51% desaturated up to maximal work in normoxia.

evidence.quote: Within 20 s of exercise onset partial myoglobin desaturation was evident even at 50% of maximum O2 consumption, was significantly greater in H than N, and was then constant at an average of 51 +/- 3% (N) and 60 +/- 3% (H) throughout the incremental exercise protocol to maximum work rate.

steps.title: Time in the capillary
steps.text:
Unloading takes time. How long a red cell stays in a capillary, its [transit time](g:transit-time), is roughly capillary blood volume ÷ blood flow. It depends on the flow, on how many capillaries there are, how many are open, and how well flow matches demand [[c:mtt-factors]].

Training raises [cardiac output](g:cardiac-output) and leg blood flow. On its own, that would rush red cells through faster and cut unloading time. But training also grows capillaries: [capillary density](g:capillary-density) typically rises by **10–30%** over 4–24 weeks, about as much as VO₂max. So transit time is probably kept about the same, despite the extra flow [[c:cap-growth]].

You met capillary growth in the muscle module; this is why it matters for oxygen.

claims.text: Red-cell capillary mean transit time is determined by blood flow, capillary density, capillary recruitment and the matching of flow to metabolic demand.

evidence.quote: the erythrocyte MTT, which is determined by the blood flow, the capillary density, the capillary recruitment and the degree of matching of blood flow distribution to the metabolic demand

claims.text: Capillary density typically rises 10–30% after 4–24 weeks of endurance training, similar to the change in VO₂max, which probably maintains transit time despite higher blood flow.

evidence.quote: Capillary density typically improves by 10‐30% after 4‐24 weeks of endurance training, which is similar to the changes in V ˙ O 2max for this training duration.
Therefore, the capillary growth probably maintains the MTT despite elevated Q ˙ max and peripheral blood flow after training.

steps.title: Does training shorten transit time?
steps.problem: After a winter of training, a cyclist's maximal leg blood flow is 15% higher and his capillary blood volume 20% higher. Transit time ∝ capillary blood volume ÷ blood flow. What happens to his transit time at maximum?
steps: Write each change as a factor: volume × 1.20, flow × 1.15.
New transit time = 1.20 ÷ 1.15 = 1.04 times the old one: 4% longer.
Without the capillary growth: 1.00 ÷ 1.15 = 0.87, so 13% shorter, and less time to unload.
Capillary growth more than makes up for the extra flow, so each red cell keeps its time to unload.

steps.title: Why extraction rises with training
steps.text:
Training can raise extraction, and mitochondria seem to matter most. A big oxidative capacity acts like a 'bottomless pit': it keeps myoglobin unloaded and PO₂ inside the fibre low, so O₂ keeps diffusing in even when capillary PO₂ is low [[c:bottomless-pit]].

In 9 people who trained one leg for 6 weeks, the trained leg extracted a little more O₂ (2–3 points) than the other. The gain tracked mitochondrial proteins, not capillaries per fibre [[c:one-leg]]. In sedentary people, 9 weeks of hard training raised leg extraction from 72% to 82% [[c:extraction-gain]].

Yet there is a floor: even in the best trained, about **10 mL O₂** stays in each litre of venous blood leaving the leg, at a PO₂ of about 10 mmHg [[c:extraction-floor]].

claims.text: A large muscle oxidative capacity keeps myoglobin saturation and intracellular PO₂ low, maintaining the capillary-to-cell PO₂ gradient and O₂ extraction even at low capillary PO₂.

evidence.quote: By analogy, the oxidative reserve capacity may act as a “bottomless pit”, keeping the myoglobin SO 2 and intracellular PO 2 low. This, in turn, maintains the PO 2 gradient between the capillary and the muscle cell, promoting O 2 diffusion and O 2 extraction even at a very low capillary PO 2 .

claims.text: After 6 weeks of one-leg knee-extension training, the trained leg had higher O₂ extraction than the control leg (largest at 83% of peak power); the difference correlated with mitochondrial proteins, not the capillary-to-fibre ratio.

evidence.quote: TL displayed higher O2 extraction than CON (main effect: 1.7 ± 1.6% points; P = .010; 40%-83% of W˙peak) with the largest between-leg difference at 83% of W˙peak

The between-leg difference in O2 extraction correlated with the between-leg ratio of citrate synthase and COX-IV (r = .72-.73; P = .03), but not with the difference in the capillary-to-fiber ratio (P = .965).

claims.text: Leg O₂ extraction fraction rose from 72% to 82% after 9 weeks of intense endurance training in previously sedentary people.

evidence.quote: an impressive increase in leg O 2 extraction fraction from 72% to 82% has been reported after only 9 weeks of intense endurance training in previously sedentary subjects

claims.text: At least about 10 mL O₂ remains in each litre of femoral venous blood, at a PO₂ of about 10 mmHg, even in the best trained, because diffusive flux becomes very small at low capillary PO₂.

evidence.quote: Hence, a minimum of ~10 mL O 2 remains in each litre of femoral venous blood associated with a PO 2 of ~10 mmHg, even for the best trained individuals.
the diffusive flux is directly proportional to the PO 2 gradient and will, thus, gradually decrease along the capillary and be very small when approaching low capillary PO 2 values such as 10 mmHg

debate.question: Does diffusion from capillary to mitochondria limit VO₂max in healthy people?

sides.position: Yes, in part: VO₂max falls in step with venous PO₂ when breathing less O₂, and a large PO₂ drop from blood to fibre points to a finite diffusing capacity.
Only a little, and less in the fit: delivery is the main limit, and muscle diffusing capacity rises with VO₂max, so diffusion limits shrink as fitness grows.

points: O₂ leaving a capillary crosses several barriers to reach the mitochondria; PO₂ falls from about 38 mmHg in the capillary to about 3 mmHg in the fibre.
Fick's law of diffusion: flux ∝ surface area × PO₂ difference, so more capillary contact means more O₂ in.
Myoglobin (P50 about 3 mmHg) pulls O₂ from haemoglobin, buffers it and helps it diffuse.
Transit time ≈ capillary volume ÷ flow; training grows capillaries about as much as flow, so red cells keep their time to unload.
Extraction rises with training, mostly through more mitochondria keeping fibre PO₂ low, but about 10 mL O₂ per litre always returns unused.

variants.stem: Along the O₂ path in a working thigh, from the air you breathe to the mitochondria, where is one of the largest drops in PO₂ at maximal effort?

options.text: From the capillary blood into the muscle fibre
options.why: Right: about 38 mmHg in the capillary against about 3 mmHg inside the fibre.

options.text: From the mitochondria to the cytoplasm
options.why: O₂ moves into the mitochondria, not out; the drop is on the way in.

options.text: Nowhere: PO₂ is about the same from capillary to mitochondria
options.why: There is a large gradient; without one, no O₂ would diffuse.

options.text: Along the artery from the heart to the thigh
options.why: PO₂ barely changes along an artery; O₂ leaves the blood in the capillaries.

variants.stem: A runner is at VO₂max. Mean PO₂ in his calf capillaries is about 38 mmHg. What is the PO₂ inside the muscle fibres most likely to be?

options.text: About 3 mmHg
options.why: Right: myoglobin-based measurements put intracellular PO₂ at about 3 mmHg at maximal effort.

options.text: About 38 mmHg, the same as the capillary
options.why: If it were the same, no O₂ would diffuse in.

options.text: About 100 mmHg, as in arterial blood
options.why: Fibre PO₂ can't be higher than capillary PO₂; O₂ flows down the gradient.

options.text: About 20 mmHg, like the venous blood
options.why: Venous PO₂ is around 20 mmHg, but the fibre is much lower still.

variants.stem: Training gives a rider's quadriceps fibres 20% more capillary contact (diffusion surface). If the PO₂ difference from blood to fibre stays the same, how does O₂ flux into the fibres change?

options.text: It rises by about 20%
options.why: Right: by Fick's law of diffusion, flux is directly proportional to surface area.

options.text: It rises by about 40%
options.why: This doubles the effect; flux is proportional to area, not to its square.

options.text: It doesn't change, as only the PO₂ difference matters
options.why: Area matters as much as the gradient in Fick's law of diffusion.

options.text: It falls, as O₂ is shared among more capillaries
options.why: More contact area raises total flux; it isn't split.

variants.stem: Late in a long triathlon run, the PO₂ difference from capillary to fibre halves while the diffusion surface stays the same. How does O₂ flux into the fibres change?

options.text: It halves
options.why: Right: flux is directly proportional to the PO₂ difference.

options.text: It falls to a quarter
options.why: Flux is proportional to the gradient, not to its square.

options.text: It stays the same, as surface area sets the flux
options.why: Surface and gradient both set flux; halving the gradient halves it.

options.text: It doubles, as O₂ moves more easily at lower pressure
options.why: A smaller pressure difference drives less O₂, not more.

variants.stem: Why does O₂ move from haemoglobin in the capillary to myoglobin inside the fibre, and not the other way?

options.text: Myoglobin binds O₂ much more tightly (P50 about 3 vs 27 mmHg)
options.why: Right: at the low PO₂ in the fibre, myoglobin still holds O₂ that haemoglobin has let go.

options.text: Myoglobin binds O₂ more loosely, so it accepts more
options.why: Looser binding (higher P50) would make it hold less, not more.

options.text: An enzyme pumps O₂ from haemoglobin to myoglobin
options.why: O₂ moves by diffusion down its pressure gradient; no pump is involved.

options.text: Myoglobin has four times as many binding sites
options.why: Myoglobin has one haem, haemoglobin four; it is affinity, not sites.

variants.stem: Name the main jobs of myoglobin in a working muscle fibre.

options.text: Store O₂, buffer it, help it diffuse to mitochondria
options.why: Right: storage, buffering of intracellular O₂ and facilitated diffusion.

options.text: Carry O₂ in blood from the lungs to the muscle
options.why: That is haemoglobin's job; myoglobin stays inside the fibre.

options.text: Make ATP from O₂ without mitochondria
options.why: Myoglobin binds O₂; ATP is made in the mitochondria.

options.text: Remove CO₂ from the fibre to the blood
options.why: CO₂ leaves by diffusion and is carried as bicarbonate; myoglobin binds O₂.

variants.stem: A runner's maximal calf blood flow rises 20% while his capillary blood volume hasn't changed yet. Transit time ∝ capillary volume ÷ flow. What happens to transit time?

options.text: About 17% shorter
options.why: Right: 1.00 ÷ 1.20 = 0.83, so 17% shorter.

options.text: 20% shorter
options.why: This subtracts the 20%; dividing by 1.20 gives a 17% fall.

options.text: 20% longer
options.why: More flow through the same volume makes transit shorter, not longer.

options.text: Unchanged
options.why: Transit time depends on flow; more flow through the same capillaries shortens it.

variants.solution: New transit = 1.00 ÷ 1.20 = 0.83 of the old: about 17% shorter.

variants.stem: After a season, a triathlete's maximal leg blood flow is 10% higher and her capillary blood volume 25% higher. Transit time ∝ capillary volume ÷ flow. What happens to transit time?

options.text: About 14% longer
15% longer
options.why: This subtracts the percentages (25 − 10); dividing the factors gives 14%.

options.text: About 12% shorter
options.why: This divides flow by volume (1.10 ÷ 1.25): the inverse.

options.text: 37.5% longer
options.why: This multiplies the factors (1.25 × 1.10) instead of dividing.

variants.solution: New transit = 1.25 ÷ 1.10 = 1.14 of the old: about 14% longer.

variants.stem: Training raises a cyclist's maximal cardiac output and leg blood flow. Why does capillary growth matter for O₂ extraction at the same time?

options.text: It keeps red cells in the capillary long enough despite faster flow
options.why: Right: more capillary volume offsets more flow, so transit time is maintained.

options.text: It raises arterial O₂ content
options.why: Capillaries don't change CaO₂; that is set by haemoglobin and the lungs.

options.text: It lowers the muscle's O₂ demand
options.why: Capillaries supply O₂; they don't reduce how much the muscle uses.

options.text: It shifts the dissociation curve to the right
options.why: Curve shifts come from acid, CO₂, heat and 2,3-DPG, not capillary number.

variants.stem: Catheters in an elite cyclist's leg at max show CaO₂ 200 mL·L⁻¹ and femoral venous content 20 mL·L⁻¹. What is his leg O₂ extraction fraction?

options.why: This is venous ÷ arterial: the share left in the blood.
This reads the a-vO₂ difference (180 mL·L⁻¹) as a percentage.
This divides arterial by the difference (200 ÷ 180); a fraction can't exceed 100%.

variants.stem: At maximal running, a runner's CaO₂ is 180 mL·L⁻¹ and her leg venous content 27 mL·L⁻¹. What is her leg O₂ extraction fraction?

options.why: This is venous ÷ arterial: the share left in the blood.
This reads the a-vO₂ difference (153 mL·L⁻¹) as a percentage.
This divides arterial by the difference (180 ÷ 153); a fraction can't exceed 100%.

variants.stem: People trained one leg for 6 weeks; the other leg was the control. The trained leg extracted more O₂, and the gain correlated with mitochondrial proteins but not with capillaries per fibre. What does this suggest?

options.text: More oxidative capacity is a main driver of higher extraction
options.why: Right: more mitochondria keep fibre PO₂ low, which keeps O₂ diffusing in.

options.text: Capillaries play no role in O₂ delivery
options.why: Capillaries matter for surface area and transit; this study just didn't link the gain to them.

options.text: Extraction rose because blood flow fell
options.why: Both legs worked at the same power, and the gain tracked mitochondrial proteins; a fall in flow wasn't what the study found.

options.text: Training changed haemoglobin only in the trained leg
options.why: Both legs share the same blood, so haemoglobin can't differ between them.

variants.stem: Why does even an elite runner's leg never extract 100% of the O₂ it receives?

options.text: Near 10 mmHg capillary PO₂, the gradient and flux become tiny
options.why: Right: about 10 mL O₂ per litre is left at a venous PO₂ of about 10 mmHg.

options.text: Haemoglobin can't release more than half its O₂
options.why: At max, extraction reaches about 90%; haemoglobin can unload far more than half.

options.text: Mitochondria stop using O₂ at the highest intensities
options.why: Mitochondria are using O₂ at their highest rate at max.

options.text: The muscle keeps some O₂ back in the blood for the brain
options.why: Each organ extracts from its own blood; the leg doesn't save O₂ for others.

variants.stem: When cyclists breathe less O₂, their VO₂max falls in a straight line with their muscle venous PO₂. One reading: diffusion from capillary to fibre limits VO₂max. What is the best judgement?

options.text: Plausible in part, but delivery stays the main limit, more so in the fit
options.why: Right: diffusion contributes, while muscle diffusing capacity rises with fitness and delivery dominates.

options.text: Proven: diffusion, not delivery, sets VO₂max
options.why: One small study of 6 men supports a diffusion component, not that diffusion is the main limit.

options.text: Impossible: diffusion can't limit VO₂max
options.why: Large blood-to-fibre PO₂ differences show diffusion has a finite capacity.

options.text: Irrelevant: breathing less O₂ changes nothing in the muscle
options.why: Lower inspired O₂ lowers arterial, capillary and venous PO₂.

variants.stem: The 3 mmHg figure for PO₂ inside working fibres comes from 6 trained men doing one-leg knee-extension in an MRI scanner. What most limits applying it to a cyclist racing at VO₂max?

options.text: One small muscle group, few people: whole-body work may differ
options.why: Right: knee-extension overperfuses a small muscle mass, unlike cycling; 6 trained men add little precision.

options.text: Myoglobin can't be measured in humans
options.why: They measured myoglobin desaturation with ¹H MR spectroscopy in humans.

options.text: Trained men have no myoglobin
options.why: Trained muscle has plenty of myoglobin.

options.text: PO₂ inside fibres is the same in every muscle and person
options.why: It varies with muscle, fibre type, training and intensity, which is why the sample matters.
